plan: Use editable weights to reveal how uncertainty changes when outcomes become more or less balanced.
title: How much uncertainty is in a distribution?
audience: Second-year engineering undergraduate familiar with logarithms and probability.

starting_point.idea: Discrete entropy measures the average surprise of an outcome.
starting_point.why: It gives a numerical way to compare uncertain and predictable sources.
starting_point.explanation: Normalize nonnegative weights into probabilities, then add each outcome's contribution. Zero-probability outcomes contribute zero. This is a small teaching example, not a reproduction of Shannon's communication experiments.

symbols.meaning: Contribution of outcome i to entropy

controls.label: Outcome weights
controls.help: Nonnegative weights are normalized into probabilities. All-zero weights use equal probabilities.

explorations.title: Make one outcome certain
explorations.instruction: Apply this preset, then inspect the bars and H.
explorations.observe: One probability is one and total entropy is zero bits.
explorations.why: A guaranteed outcome carries no surprise.

explorations.title: Make four outcomes equally likely
explorations.instruction: Apply this preset, then compare the four contributions and H.
explorations.observe: Each outcome contributes half a bit; total entropy is two bits.
explorations.why: Four equally likely outcomes require two binary choices to identify one.

limitation: The weights are teaching controls, not frequencies measured from Shannon's paper. When all active weights are zero, this toy model chooses a uniform distribution so the calculation remains defined.

grounding.paper: C. E. Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication
grounding.claim: Entropy is the sum of negative probability times base-two log probability.
Editable weights are normalized to make a valid probability distribution.

tests.name: four equal outcomes give two bits

compute_js: function compute(inputs) { const count = Math.max(1, Math.min(4, Math.round(inputs.count))); const active = inputs.weights.slice(0, count); const total = active.reduce((sum, value) => sum + value, 0); const probabilities = total === 0 ? active.map(() => 1 / count) : active.map(value => value / total); const contributions = probabilities.map(p => p === 0 ? 0 : -p * Math.log2(p)); const entropy_bits = contributions.reduce((sum, value) => sum + value, 0); return { probabilities, contributions, entropy_bits }; }
